THOUGHT: This 8-month-old boy presents with subacute onset of feeding difficulties, abdominal distension, and paradoxical weight gain despite reduced oral intake—suggesting caloric retention or fluid accumulation rather than malnutrition. His irritability and intense crying upon abdominal palpation—especially localized to the left lower quadrant—point to discomfort from distension or obstruction. Physical exam reveals a soft but distended abdomen with tympany in the left lower quadrant, consistent with gas accumulation proximal to an obstructive site. Crucially, the abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops and absence of rectal gas—a classic “empty rectum” sign highly suggestive of functional or mechanical distal colonic obstruction. The barium enema demonstrates a transition zone in the distal colon, which is the radiographic hallmark of Hirschsprung disease (HD): a congenital aganglionosis of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, most commonly affecting the rectosigmoid region. HD typically presents in infancy with constipation, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium (though this patient was born at term without noted neonatal complications—some milder or short-segment cases may present later, as in this 8-month-old). The absence of fever, leukocytosis, vomiting, or diarrhea makes infectious, inflammatory, or acute surgical causes (e.g., intussusception, volvulus, sepsis) less likely. Weight gain despite poor feeding can occur in HD due to chronic low-grade intestinal obstruction leading to fluid retention, bacterial overgrowth with increased calorie absorption, or parental supplementation (e.g., frequent small feeds or high-calorie formulas) in response to fussiness—yet the radiographic and contrast study findings are definitive. The transition zone on barium enema is highly specific for HD; confirmation would be via rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells, but clinically and radiographically, this is diagnostic.

DIAGNOSIS: Hirschsprung disease
